theory_mcq.question: What is the OVERLAP CONDITION between intervals [a,b] and [c,d], and what is the equivalent NON-OVERLAP condition?
options: Overlap: a < c; Non-overlap: a >= c

OVERLAP: a <= d AND c <= b — each interval's start is before or at the other's end; NON-OVERLAP (complement): b < c OR d < a — one interval ends entirely before the other starts; the overlap condition is easier to compute via the non-overlap negation: `!(a[1] < b[0] || b[1] < a[0])`; note that touching intervals (e.g., [1,2] and [2,3]) ARE considered overlapping since 2<=2 satisfies the condition
Overlap: a == c; Non-overlap: a != c
Overlap: b > c; Non-overlap: b <= c
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concepts: 'Overlap condition: two intervals [a,b] and [c,d] overlap if a <= d AND c <= b' and 'Non-overlap: b < c OR d < a (one ends before the other starts)' — the lesson's code uses the negation form `!(a[1] < b[0] || b[1] < a[0])` which is logically equivalent; touching intervals (b==c) are overlapping.

theory_mcq.question: After SORTING by start time, why does the interval scan only need to compare each interval with the PREVIOUS interval (not all prior intervals)?
options: The scan must compare with all prior intervals; sorting only speeds up the initial check

After sorting by start, any interval i's start >= all previous intervals' starts; the only potential overlap is with the interval that has the LATEST END among all processed intervals — which is tracked by the current merge window or the last-kept interval; a new interval starting at time t cannot overlap with any previous interval ending before t (they ended too early); it can only potentially overlap with the one having the latest end, which we track explicitly
Sorting ensures no two intervals can overlap at all
The comparison is with the next interval, not the previous one
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'After sorting: only need to compare each interval with the previous one' — sorting enables the key simplification: since intervals are ordered by start time, any new interval either overlaps with the most recently added/merged interval (the one with the maximum end seen so far) or starts a new non-overlapping group; intervals further back in the result list ended earlier and cannot overlap.

logic_mcq.question: For `mergePattern([[1,3],[2,6],[8,10],[15,18]])`, trace the merge scan. What happens at interval [2,6]?
options: [2,6] starts a new merged interval since 2 > 3

After sorting (already sorted), result=[[[1,3]]]; processing [2,6]: start=2 <= prev[1]=3 → OVERLAP; prev[1]=max(3,6)=6; result=[[[1,6]]]; then [8,10]: start=8 > 6 → new interval; result=[[[1,6],[8,10]]]; then [15,18]: new; result=[[[1,6],[8,10],[15,18]]] — confirmed by direct execution
[2,6] extends the interval to [1,3+6=9]
The scan skips [2,6] because it starts inside [1,3]
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution: mergePattern returns [[1,6],[8,10],[15,18]]; at [2,6]: curr[0]=2 <= prev[1]=3 (overlap detected); prev[1] updated to max(3,6)=6; the merged interval [1,6] replaces [1,3] in the result.

logic_mcq.question: For `resourcePattern([[0,30],[5,10],[15,20]])`, trace the heap state after each meeting. How many rooms are needed?
options: 3 rooms needed: each meeting requires a separate room

Sorted by start: [0,30],[5,10],[15,20]; [0,30]: heap empty → push 30, heap=[30], rooms=1; [5,10]: heap[0]=30 > 5 → no free room → push 10, heap=[10,30], rooms=2; [15,20]: heap sorted=[10,30], heap[0]=10 ≤ 15 → room free! remove 10, push 20, heap=[20,30], rooms=2; answer=2 — confirmed by direct execution
1 room: meetings can all be scheduled sequentially
2 rooms during first half but 3 at the peak
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution and matching the lesson's trace: heap after [0,30]=[30]; after [5,10]=[10,30] (room 30 not free, need new room); after [15,20]: 10<=15 so room 10 freed and reused for 20 → heap=[20,30]; size=2.

syntax_mcq.question: The sort comparator `(a,b) => a[0] !== b[0] ? a[0]-b[0] : a[1]-b[1]` sorts by start then by end for ties. Why sort by end for ties?
options: Tie-breaking by end is required for correctness in all interval algorithms

When two intervals share the SAME START TIME, sorting by end time ascending ensures the shorter interval comes first; this tie-breaking matters in specific algorithms (like Non-Overlapping Intervals sorted by end, or Insert Interval) but is primarily a STABILITY/DETERMINISM convention; for Merge Intervals, tie-breaking doesn't affect correctness since both orderings of same-start intervals produce the same merged result; the secondary sort makes the behavior deterministic and consistent
Tie-breaking by end ensures O(n log n) instead of O(n²) time complexity
Tie-breaking is required to prevent infinite loops in the scan
syntax_mcq.explanation: Secondary sort by end time for ties is a convention for deterministic output; for Merge Intervals specifically, the order of same-start intervals doesn't affect the final merged result (both get merged regardless); for Non-Overlapping Intervals and similar problems that are sensitive to ordering within ties, consistent tie-breaking ensures deterministic correct output.

theory_mcq.question: Why does the merge condition use `start <= prev[1]` (not `start < prev[1]`) to detect overlap?
options: < is correct; using <= is a bug that merges touching intervals incorrectly

TOUCHING INTERVALS (e.g., [1,4] and [4,5]) ARE considered overlapping in Merge Intervals: the interval [1,4] ends at 4 and [4,5] starts at 4; they share a point; using `start <= prev[1]` correctly merges them into [1,5]; using `start < prev[1]` would treat [4,5] as non-overlapping with [1,4] and output [[1,4],[4,5]] which violates the problem definition that touching intervals merge
The <= condition only matters for floating-point intervals
start <= prev[1] is used for performance; < would also be correct
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's example: 'merge [[1,4],[4,5]]: [[1,5]] (touching = overlap)' — the condition `start <= prev[1]` captures both true overlaps (start < prev[1]) and touching intervals (start == prev[1]); the lesson confirms touching as overlap; using strict < would incorrectly separate touching intervals.

theory_mcq.question: Why does the merge use `Math.max(prev[1], curr[1])` instead of just `curr[1]` when extending the end?
options: curr[1] is always larger than prev[1] after sorting; Math.max is redundant

CONTAINMENT: if one interval is fully inside another (e.g., [1,4] followed by [2,3]), curr[1]=3 < prev[1]=4; using just `curr[1]` would SHRINK the merged interval to [1,3] (incorrect); `Math.max(prev[1], curr[1])` correctly handles both the standard overlap case (curr[1] > prev[1] → extend) and the containment case (curr[1] < prev[1] → keep prev[1] unchanged)
Math.max is only needed when intervals are in descending order
curr[1] is always correct; Math.max prevents array reallocation
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's example: 'merge [[1,4],[2,3]]: [[1,4]] (containment)' and concept 'Math.max(prev[1], curr[1]): handles both overlap and containment' — after sorting by start, intervals with the same start or overlapping starts can have their end before the current merged end; Math.max ensures the merged interval never shrinks.

logic_mcq.question: For `insert([[1,3],[6,9]], [2,5])`, trace the three phases. Which intervals are added in each phase?
options: Phase 1 (before): nothing (2<1[1]=3? No); Phase 2 (overlap): merge with [1,3] and [2,5]→[1,5]; Phase 3 (after): [6,9]; result [[1,5],[6,9]] ✓
Phase 1: add [1,3]; Phase 2: add [2,5]; Phase 3: add [6,9]; result [[1,3],[2,5],[6,9]]
Phase 1: add nothing; Phase 2: no merge; Phase 3: add all
Phase 1: add [6,9]; Phase 2: merge [1,3] and [2,5]; Phase 3: nothing
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution: insert([[1,3],[6,9]],[2,5])=[[1,5],[6,9]]; Phase 1: i=0, intervals[0][1]=3 >= ns=2 → stop immediately (no intervals end before new starts); Phase 2: intervals[0][0]=1<=mergedE=5 → merge: mergedS=min(2,1)=1, mergedE=max(5,3)=5, i=1; intervals[1][0]=6>mergedE=5 → stop; push [1,5]; Phase 3: push [6,9].

logic_mcq.question: For `insert([[1,2],[3,5],[6,7],[8,10],[12,16]], [4,8])`, which existing intervals does [4,8] overlap with?
options: [4,8] overlaps only with [3,5]

[4,8] overlaps with [3,5] (4<=5), [6,7] (6<=8), and [8,10] (8<=8 touching); Phase 2 merges all three: mergedS=min(4,3)=3, mergedE=max(8,5,7,10)=10; result [[1,2],[3,10],[12,16]] — confirmed by direct execution
[4,8] overlaps with all intervals
[4,8] creates a new standalone interval; no merging occurs
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution: [[1,2],[3,10],[12,16]]; Phase 1 adds [1,2] (ends at 2 < ns=4); Phase 2: [3,5]: 3<=mergedE=8→merge to [3,8]; [6,7]: 6<=8→merge to [3,8] (max(8,7)=8); [8,10]: 8<=8 (touching)→merge to [3,10]; [12,16]: 12>10→stop; push [3,10]; Phase 3: push [12,16].

syntax_mcq.question: In Merge Intervals, `const result = [intervals[0].slice()]` creates a SHALLOW COPY of the first interval. Why is `.slice()` (or spread) needed here?
options: slice() converts the array to a string for faster comparison

Without `.slice()`, `result[0]` would be the SAME REFERENCE as `intervals[0]`; when the merge algorithm later modifies `result[result.length-1][1]` to extend the end, it would MUTATE the original `intervals[0]` array (a side effect violating immutability); `.slice()` creates an independent copy of the [start, end] pair so the result array can be modified freely without affecting the input intervals
slice() is required because intervals are stored as linked lists
slice() converts the interval from 1-indexed to 0-indexed
syntax_mcq.explanation: Defensive copying is critical here: `result.push([start, end])` for new intervals creates fresh arrays, but the first interval is directly referenced via `intervals[0]` without `.slice()` it would be the same object; subsequent `prev[1] = Math.max(...)` would mutate `intervals[0][1]` in-place, which is a hidden side effect; `.slice()` or `[...intervals[0]]` ensures the first element is an independent copy.

theory_mcq.question: Why does Non-Overlapping Intervals sort by END TIME (not start time), and why is this critical for the greedy strategy?
options: End time sorting is identical to start time sorting for this problem

SORT BY END enables the EARLIEST-ENDING greedy: keeping the interval with the smallest end time leaves the MOST ROOM for future intervals; an interval with a smaller end creates less future conflict; if instead we sorted by start and kept the first interval (e.g., [1,10]), we'd block all future intervals starting before 10 even though a shorter interval [2,3] would leave more space; the lesson's counterexample: sort by end on [[1,10],[2,3],[3,4]] keeps [2,3] and [3,4], removing only [1,10] — optimal
Sort by end is just a convention; sort by start produces the same result
Sort by end is required to handle touching intervals correctly
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's proof-by-example: 'Sort by START: keep [1,10], conflict [2,3] remove, conflict [3,4] remove → remove=2; Sort by END: [[2,3],[3,4],[1,10]] keep [2,3], keep [3,4] (3>=3), conflict [1,10] remove → remove=1 ✓' — earliest-end greedy is provably optimal via exchange argument.

theory_mcq.question: How is Non-Overlapping Intervals related to MINIMUM ARROWS TO BURST BALLOONS?
options: They are completely different problems requiring different algorithms

Both use the SAME GREEDY STRUCTURE: sort by end time, scan left to right tracking the current 'boundary'; in Non-Overlapping Intervals: when a conflict occurs, increment remove count (don't update lastEnd); in Min Arrows: when a balloon starts AFTER the current arrow position, fire a new arrow (increment arrows, update arrowPos to new balloon's end); the key difference is the condition: Non-Overlapping uses `start >= lastEnd` (>=, touching = non-conflicting); Min Arrows uses `start > arrowPos` (>, touching means the arrow still hits both balloons)
Min Arrows is a 2D problem; Non-Overlapping is 1D
Both problems always have the same numerical answer for the same input
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's connection: both sort by end time; both use the 'keep the earliest-ending interval/arrow' greedy; the structural difference is: Non-Overlapping keeps an interval and updates lastEnd when no conflict; Min Arrows fires an arrow at the current balloon's end when a new balloon starts after the current arrow; touching creates a conflict in arrows (> not >=) but not in non-overlapping (>= not >).

logic_mcq.question: For `eraseOverlapIntervals([[1,2],[2,3],[3,4],[1,3]])`, after sorting by end, what is the order and how many are removed?
options: Sorted: [[1,3],[1,2],[2,3],[3,4]]; all overlap, remove 3
The intervals are already non-overlapping; removed=0
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution returning 1; after sort by end: [[1,2],[2,3],[1,3],[3,4]]; kept=1, lastEnd=2; [2,3]: start=2>=lastEnd=2→keep, lastEnd=3, kept=2; [1,3]: start=1<lastEnd=3→conflict, skip; [3,4]: start=3>=3→keep, kept=3; removed=4-3=1.

logic_mcq.question: The lesson states Non-Overlapping Intervals is connected to LIS (Longest Increasing Subsequence). What is the connection?
options: Both use binary search on a sorted array

Non-Overlapping Intervals asks for the MAXIMUM NUMBER OF NON-OVERLAPPING INTERVALS TO KEEP — which is equivalent to finding the longest chain of intervals where each interval starts at or after the previous ends; this 'longest chain of compatible intervals' is structurally identical to LIS: treating intervals as sequence elements where 'compatible' replaces 'increasing'; both problems can be solved with the same greedy (earliest-end strategy for intervals = patience sorting for LIS) or O(n²) DP
Both problems always require sorting by start time
LIS only applies when all intervals have unit length
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Connection to LIS: same greedy structure' — the maximum number of non-overlapping intervals (n - eraseOverlapIntervals) is the 'interval scheduling maximisation' problem, a classic whose structure mirrors LIS; both select the longest sequence satisfying a compatibility condition, solvable by the same greedy or DP approaches.

syntax_mcq.question: The conflict check uses `start >= lastEnd` (>=, not >) for Non-Overlapping Intervals but `start > arrowPos` (>) for Min Arrows. What is the semantic difference?
options: Both should use >= for consistency; using > is a bug in Min Arrows

TOUCHING INTERVALS are treated differently: in Non-Overlapping Intervals, [1,2] and [2,3] TOUCHING at point 2 is NOT a conflict (you can keep both, start at 2 after ending at 2); `>=` correctly allows touching; in Min Arrows, an arrow AT position 2 hits BOTH [1,2] and [2,3] simultaneously (they share point 2); so a balloon starting at arrowPos is still hit by the current arrow; `>` correctly fires a new arrow only when the balloon starts STRICTLY after the current arrow
The difference is due to 0-indexed vs 1-indexed arrays
Both conditions are equivalent for integer intervals
syntax_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concepts: for Non-Overlapping Intervals, `start >= lastEnd` means touching (sharing an endpoint) is non-conflicting (both intervals can coexist); for Min Arrows, `start > arrowPos` means an arrow at position p hits any balloon with start <= p <= end, so a balloon starting exactly at arrowPos is already covered by the current arrow; the semantics of 'conflict' differ between the two problems.

theory_mcq.question: In Meeting Rooms II, the min-heap stores END TIMES. What does removing `heap[0]` when `heap[0] <= start` represent physically?
options: Removing the earliest end time represents destroying a room permanently

Removing `heap[0]` represents REUSING THE ROOM whose meeting ended earliest — if the earliest-ending meeting finishes at time heap[0] and the new meeting starts at time 'start' >= heap[0], that room is NOW FREE; removing its old end time and adding the new meeting's end time represents the same room transitioning from its old meeting to the new one; if no room is free (heap[0] > start), we add a new room (push without removing), increasing the room count
Removing heap[0] represents cancelling the current meeting
heap[0] is the room number, not the end time
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's trace comment: 'Reuse room whose meeting ends earliest if it finishes before this starts' — the heap models 'rooms in use, identified by when their current meeting ends'; when heap[0] (smallest end time) <= new meeting's start, that room is free; removing its end time and adding the new end time represents booking the same physical room for the new meeting.

theory_mcq.question: Meeting Rooms I uses `intervals[i][0] < intervals[i-1][1]` for conflict detection. Why `<` (not `<=`)?
options: Using < is wrong; <= should be used for correctness

A conflict for ONE PERSON attending ALL MEETINGS means two meetings OVERLAP IN TIME — not just touch; if meeting A ends at time 5 and meeting B starts at time 5, one person can finish A and immediately start B (back-to-back meetings are OK for one person); `start < prev_end` means B starts BEFORE A ends (actual time overlap = can't attend both); `start <= prev_end` would incorrectly reject touching meetings where one person can attend both consecutively
< is used because meetings are stored in 0-indexed arrays
< is a convention; both < and <= produce the same result for integer times
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson: canAttendMeetings checks `intervals[i][0] < intervals[i-1][1]` — strict less-than means 'starts before the previous ends'; meeting A ending at exactly time T and meeting B starting at T is NOT a conflict (one person can attend back-to-back); this contrasts with Meeting Rooms II where `heap[0] <= start` (<=) means a room is free when a meeting ends at exactly the new start time.

logic_mcq.question: For `minMeetingRooms([[0,30],[5,10],[15,20]])`, trace the heap state precisely. When does [15,20] reuse a room?
options: [15,20] always needs a new room; 3 rooms are needed

After sorting by start: [0,30],[5,10],[15,20]; after [0,30]: heap=[30], rooms=1; after [5,10]: heap[0]=30>5→no free, push 10→heap=[10,30], rooms=2; after [15,20]: sort heap→[10,30], heap[0]=10≤15→free room! shift 10, push 20→heap=[20,30], rooms=2; ANSWER=2 — [15,20] reuses the room that had [5,10]
[15,20] reuses the room that had [0,30]
All three meetings are simultaneous; 3 rooms needed
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution and the lesson's explicit trace: the room that held [5,10] (ending at time 10) is free when [15,20] starts at 15 (10<=15); that room is reused for [15,20]; [0,30] is still ongoing when [15,20] starts (30>15), so that room remains occupied; final heap=[20,30], size=2.

logic_mcq.question: The TWO SORTED ARRAYS alternative approach for Meeting Rooms II tracks a `rooms` counter and `endPtr`. Why does `endPtr` advance when `start >= ends[endPtr]` (not when `start > ends[endPtr]`)?
options: endPtr should advance on > not >=; using >= is a bug

When a meeting ends at time ends[endPtr] and a new meeting starts at time start with start >= ends[endPtr], the room is FREE (meeting ended AT or BEFORE new start); advancing endPtr marks this room as reused; if start == ends[endPtr], the room ended exactly at the new start time (touching = can reuse); if start > ends[endPtr], the room ended before the new start (can definitely reuse); `>=` correctly captures both cases; NOT advancing endPtr (leaving rooms++) would incorrectly add a new room when one is actually available
endPtr advances on >=  only for meetings with even start times
endPtr and rooms are independent; endPtr advancement has no effect on rooms
logic_mcq.explanation: In the two-sorted-arrays approach: `if (start < ends[endPtr]) rooms++` (new room needed); `else endPtr++` (reuse: advance past the freed end time); the condition `start < ends[endPtr]` (equivalent to `start >= ends[endPtr]` for reuse) matches the min-heap approach where `heap[0] <= start` frees a room; both use non-strict comparison for 'ended at exactly start time = free'.

syntax_mcq.question: In the heap-based Meeting Rooms II, the heap is sorted (O(n log n)) at each iteration. The lesson notes 'use proper MinHeap in production'. What makes a proper MinHeap better?
options: A proper MinHeap produces different results than the sorted-array approach

A PROPER MIN-HEAP (e.g., binary heap) provides O(log n) insertion and O(log n) extraction of the minimum; the lesson's array-sort approach costs O(n log n) PER INSERTION (re-sorting the entire heap each time); for n meetings: O(n²log n) total vs O(n log n) with a proper heap; both produce IDENTICAL RESULTS but the heap is orders of magnitude faster for large inputs; the sort-based approach is pedagogically clear for interviews but inappropriate for production code
A proper MinHeap uses less memory than an array
Only a proper MinHeap can correctly identify the earliest-ending meeting
syntax_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's note: 'heap.sort() for interview clarity; use proper MinHeap in production' — the sort-based approach sorts the entire array at each step (O(n log n) per meeting), giving O(n² log n) total; a proper binary min-heap maintains heap-order property with O(log n) push/pop operations, achieving O(n log n) total for all n meetings; both are correct, but production code requires the proper implementation.

theory_mcq.question: In Jump Game I, why is checking `if (i > maxReach) return false` BEFORE updating maxReach the correct order?
options: The order doesn't matter; maxReach can be checked after updating

If `i > maxReach`, position i is UNREACHABLE — no previous jump could reach it; there is no point updating maxReach from position i (we can't be at position i to jump from it); checking BEFORE the update immediately returns false when stuck, without performing a meaningless maxReach update from an unreachable position; if the check came AFTER the update, we'd compute `maxReach = max(maxReach, i + nums[i])` from a position we can't actually reach, potentially giving a false optimistic maxReach
Updating maxReach before checking prevents off-by-one errors
The order is irrelevant; the check and update are in the same loop body
theory_mcq.explanation: The if-then-update order enforces the 'can we reach position i?' invariant: only if i <= maxReach can we actually be at i and make a jump; checking first ensures we immediately detect unreachability; updating first would use nums[i] from an unreachable position — semantically invalid (you can't jump from a position you can't reach).

theory_mcq.question: In Jump Game II, what do `curEnd` and `farthest` represent, and why is the loop `for (let i = 0; i < nums.length - 1; i)` (not including the last index)?
options: curEnd is the current position; farthest is the target; the loop excludes the last index arbitrarily

`curEnd` = the BOUNDARY of positions reachable by the current number of jumps; `farthest` = the FARTHEST position reachable from any position in [0..curEnd]; when i reaches curEnd, we MUST jump to extend the reach to farthest — this counts as one more jump; the loop excludes `nums.length - 1` because we don't need to jump FROM the last position (we've already arrived); including it would increment jumps unnecessarily when already at or past the target
curEnd is the start of the current window; farthest is the current position
The loop excludes the last index to prevent array out-of-bounds
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's trace and concepts: curEnd marks the reachability frontier of the current jump level; farthest tracks the best next frontier; when i==curEnd, we've exhausted positions at the current level and must jump; excluding `nums.length-1` prevents a spurious jump increment when we've already confirmed reaching the destination.

logic_mcq.question: Trace `jump([2,3,1,1,4])`. What are curEnd, farthest, and jumps at each step?
options: i=0: far=2, i==curEnd(0)→jumps=1, curEnd=2; i=1: far=max(2,4)=4, i<2; i=2: far=4, i==curEnd(2)→jumps=2, curEnd=4>=4 break; return 2 ✓
i=0: jump immediately, jumps=1; i=1: jump, jumps=2; answer=2
The algorithm scans all 5 positions before returning 3 jumps
i=0: far=2; i=1: far=4; i=2: jump; i=3: jump; return 4 jumps
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution returning 2 and matching the lesson's exact trace: 'i=0: farthest=max(0,0+2)=2. i==curEnd(0): jumps=1, curEnd=2. i=1: farthest=max(2,1+3)=4. i<curEnd(2). i=2: farthest=max(4,2+1)=4. i==curEnd(2): jumps=2, curEnd=4>=4: break. Answer: 2 jumps.'

logic_mcq.question: For Gas Station `gas=[1,2,3,4,5]`, `cost=[3,4,5,1,2]`, explain why starting at station 3 (index 3) works.
options: Station 3 works because it has the most gas (gas[3]=4)

Net gains: [1-3=-2, 2-4=-2, 3-5=-2, 4-1=3, 5-2=3]; from station 3: net=3 (reach 4), net=3 (reach 0), net=-2 (reach 1), net=-2 (reach 2), net=-2 (reach 3=start); running sum from 3: 3→6→4→2→0; never goes negative; total net=sum=(-2+-2+-2+3+3)=-1+5=1>0 so a solution exists; the greedy correctly sets start=3 because curr goes negative at stations 0,1,2 — confirmed by direct execution returning 3
Station 3 is the last station; we always start from the last
Any station with positive net gain can be the start
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution: canCompleteCircuit([1,2,3,4,5],[3,4,5,1,2])=3; total net=1>=0 (solution exists); the greedy resets start whenever curr<0: after station 0 (curr=-2<0), start=1; after station 1 (curr=-2<0), start=2; after station 2 (curr=-2<0), start=3; stations 3 and 4 keep curr positive; start=3 is the answer.

syntax_mcq.question: In Gas Station, `total >= 0 ? start : -1` is returned. Why does `total >= 0` guarantee a solution EXISTS (not just that `start` is valid)?
options: total >= 0 means the specific start station will always work

If `total >= 0`, the SUM OF ALL NET GAINS is non-negative — meaning the circuit provides at least as much gas as it costs globally; a classic result in circular-array problems: if the total is non-negative, the greedy start point (the last reset point) is ALWAYS a valid starting station; this is because the greedy ensures: (1) all stations before `start` were 'dead ends' (caused curr to go negative), (2) from `start` onward, curr stayed non-negative; together with total>=0, the wrap-around (going through earlier stations after completing the circuit from start) is also guaranteed sufficient
total >= 0 only means a partial circuit is possible, not a full one
total >= 0 is a necessary but not sufficient condition; additional checks are needed
syntax_mcq.explanation: The proof sketch: if total >= 0, the greedy algorithm guarantees the last `start` value is a valid starting station; intuitively, the segments before `start` all caused curr to go negative (they're locally insufficient), but the global total being non-negative means the 'positive tail' (stations from `start` onward) compensates for the 'negative prefix'; this is the greedy correctness proof for Gas Station.

theory_mcq.question: What is the EXCHANGE ARGUMENT proof technique, and how does it prove greedy optimality?
options: The exchange argument shows that greedy is always faster than DP

EXCHANGE ARGUMENT: assume there exists an OPTIMAL SOLUTION that differs from the greedy solution at some point; show that you can SWAP the optimal choice at that point with the greedy choice without WORSENING the result (the number of kept intervals/jumps/etc. stays the same or improves); by repeatedly applying swaps, the optimal solution is transformed into the greedy solution while never decreasing quality — proving greedy is AT LEAST AS GOOD as optimal
The exchange argument proves greedy always beats DP by a constant factor
Exchange argument shows two solutions have equal cost by induction on input size
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Exchange argument: assume an optimal solution; show that any deviation from greedy can be swapped to the greedy choice without worsening the result' — the lesson demonstrates this for Non-Overlapping Intervals: swapping an interval with a later end for one with an earlier end cannot decrease the kept count; for Jump Game II: swapping a shorter jump for the greedy farthest cannot increase the jump count.

theory_mcq.question: The lesson shows greedy FAILS for Coin Change (coins=[1,3,4], target=6). What is the formal reason?
options: Coin change fails because coins are not sorted

The EXCHANGE ARGUMENT FAILS for coin change: taking the largest coin (4) blocks the 2-coin (3+3) solution; swapping the greedy choice (4) for the optimal choice (3) IMPROVES the result (needs fewer coins) — the swap argument goes in the wrong direction; formally, the greedy doesn't have the MATROID structure that guarantees optimality; the locally-optimal choice (largest coin = fewest immediate coins used) doesn't lead to the globally-optimal choice (minimum total coins)
Greedy fails only when coins are not powers of 2
Greedy always fails for coin change regardless of denominations
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's example: 'Greedy takes 4, leaving 2 → takes 1,1 → 3 coins. Optimal: 3+3 = 2 coins. Exchange argument FAILS: taking largest coin (4) blocks the 2-coin solution' — the exchange argument in the reverse direction (swap greedy choice 4 for optimal choice 3) IMPROVES the result, meaning greedy is NOT optimal; this is why DP is required for coin change.

logic_mcq.question: For `partitionLabels('ababcbacadefegdehijhklij')`, the answer is [9,7,8]. Trace why the first partition has length 9.
options: The first 'a' appears at index 0; the first partition ends at its last occurrence

Character 'a' appears at indices 0,2,4,7,8 (last=8); 'b' appears at 1,3,5 (last=5); 'c' appears at 6 (last=6); the partition must extend to include ALL occurrences of every character it contains; starting at 0, the end is extended as each character's last occurrence is checked: max(last['a']=8, last['b']=5, last['c']=6)=8; at i=8 (==end=8), partition closes with length 8-0+1=9; confirmed by direct execution
The first partition contains exactly 9 distinct characters
The first partition ends when a space character is found
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution: partitionLabels('ababcbacadefegdehijhklij')=[9,7,8]; first partition: start=0, end tracked by max(last[s[i]]) for i=0..8; last['a']=8, last['b']=5, last['c']=6; end reaches 8 at i=2 (last['a']); when i==end==8, partition length=8-0+1=9, start=9.

syntax_mcq.question: In `partitionLabels`, `end = Math.max(end, last[s[i]])` extends the partition boundary. Why is `if (i === end)` used as the partition-close condition rather than checking if `i === last[s[i]]`?
options: Both conditions are equivalent; the choice is stylistic

`i === end` checks whether we've reached the CURRENT PARTITION BOUNDARY (the maximum last-occurrence of any character seen so far in this partition); `i === last[s[i]]` only checks if the CURRENT CHARACTER's last occurrence is here — but the partition can't close until ALL characters started in this partition have had their last occurrence included; `end` tracks the maximum over all characters, ensuring the partition includes all occurrences of all contained characters; closing at `last[s[i]]` would incorrectly split partitions too early when other characters have later occurrences
i===last[s[i]] would work if the string had no repeated characters
i===end is needed to prevent negative partition lengths
syntax_mcq.explanation: The partition boundary `end` is the MAXIMUM of all `last[character]` values for characters seen so far; when i reaches end, every character that started in this partition has had its FINAL OCCURRENCE at or before index end; closing the partition at `i===last[s[i]]` would close prematurely if another character in the same partition has a later last occurrence — `end` correctly tracks the global maximum.
